Roxadustat for treatment of suspected erythropoietin(EPO)-induced pure red cell aplasia in a hemodialysis patient: a case report
abstract: Abstract Anemia is a prevalent complication in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), particularly those undergoing dialysis. Recombinant human erythropoietin (rhEPO) is widely administered to patients both on and off dialysis to manage this anemia. However, despite an initial favorable therapeutic response, a sudden and unexplained decline in hemoglobin levels (Hb) often prompts the need for further diagnostic evaluation. In this context, we report a clinical case involving a 48-year-old male patient who had been undergoing hemodialysis (HD) for two years. During the course of his rhEPO treatment regimen, he developed pure red cell aplasia (PRCA), a rare but serious adverse reaction. Upon recognition of this complication, the administration of rhEPO was promptly discontinued, and the patient was initiated on roxarestat therapy. Remarkably, following nine months of continuous roxarestat treatment, the patient experienced a significant and sustained increase in his Hb levels. This clinical outcome underscores the importance of prompt diagnosis and intervention in cases of EPO-induced PRCA. Furthermore, our findings suggest that roxarestat may serve as a viable and effective therapeutic option for patients with EPO-induced PRCA, potentially obviating the need for immunosuppressive therapy and its associated risks.

title: Heterogeneous cost-control pathways of DRG payment reform and associated risks in stroke care: A multicentre quasi-experimental study
abstract: Abstract Background China's DRG payment reform targets healthcare cost containment, yet whether cost reductions translate into genuine efficiency gains or billing adaptation—and what this means for clinical quality and patient financial protection—remains unclear, particularly across hospitals of varying institutional capacity. Methods We analyzed 2019 and 2023 discharge records from three tertiary hospitals representing distinct economic development contexts: Dalian (developed, n = 13,726), Zhuzhou (mid-income, n = 7,297), and Zhumadian (underdeveloped, n = 12,391). Propensity score matching, interrupted time series, quantile regression, mediation analysis, and Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition were applied to characterise reform effects and mechanisms. Monte Carlo simulation across ten periods and five policy scenarios projected counterfactual outcomes. Results Mean hospitalisation costs fell by 11.1% at Dalian, 20.1% at Zhuzhou, and 36.3% at Zhumadian (pooled − 23.2%; I²=99.4%). At Dalian, pharmaceutical costs fell from 33.4% to 18.2% while diagnostic imaging and nursing shares were preserved; mediation analysis attributed 62.1% of the cost reduction to clinical pathway changes. At Zhumadian, pharmaceutical expenditure dropped by 27.6 percentage points but was largely offset by expansion of "other costs" from 30.2% to 64.8%; only 30.1% of the reduction was mediated through clinical pathways. Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition revealed that 85.2% of cross-site cost differentials stemmed from hospital behavioural differences rather than patient case-mix. In-hospital mortality declined uniformly across sites (adjusted ORs 0.60–0.64). However, hospital-acquired pneumonia and deep vein thrombosis rates increased at Zhuzhou and Zhumadian (adjusted ORs 1.42–1.73; E-values 2.21–2.89). Out-of-pocket expenditure decreased at Dalian (− 8.3%) but rose at Zhumadian (+ 9.4%), where catastrophic health expenditure increased from 24.6% to 31.2% despite the largest absolute cost reduction. Simulation showed that DRG alone raised the quality risk index to 0.114 by period nine, whereas coupling DRG with behavioural regulation held the index at 0.105 while achieving greater cost reduction (− 13.6%). Conclusions DRG reform achieved cost containment through different mechanisms depending on institutional context. Where governance capacity was limited, cost reductions were driven largely by expenditure reclassification rather than care optimisation, and were accompanied by deterioration in nursing-sensitive quality indicators and worsening patient financial burden. Effective implementation requires differentiated strategies that match governance investment to institutional capacity and ensure that insurance benefit design keeps pace with payment reform.

title: Perceived Workload and Human Factors Among Healthcare Professionals During Humanitarian and Global Health Outreach Initiatives: A Scoping Review
abstract: This scoping review maps structured multidimensional perceived-workload measurement among healthcare professionals working in humanitarian and global health outreach, short-term medical missions, disaster medical deployments, and comparable field-based healthcare activities. Based on JBI methodology and reported according to PRISMA-ScR, it distinguishes direct humanitarian/outreach workload studies from transferable real-world prehospital/EMS workload measurement and a separate contextual literature on burnout, fatigue, stress, and other human factors. Outcomes include instruments, workload components, timing and frequency of measurement, use of usual-work references, and operational correlates. Two independent reviewers will screen and chart studies. No meta-analysis is planned. Initial searches began in October 2026; PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov searches were run on November 17, 2026. Independent Reviewer 2 screening, remaining native database searches, study selection, and synthesis are pending.
